top_result_summaries.title: CDC reports over 2,000 US measles cases after recent outbreaks
top_result_summaries.snippet: # US has passed 2K measles cases this year. The number of U.S. measles cases in 2026 has now exceeded 2,000, quickly approaching the full annual total of last year. As of June 4, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has confirmed 2,030 cases so far this year, with 93 percent — or 1,890 cases — associated with outbreaks. Throughout all of 2025, the CDC confirmed 2,288 measles cases. Thirty new measles outbreaks have been confirmed this year. Measles cases have been reported by 40 jurisdictions with only 10 so far reported by international visitors to the U.S. At the current rate, the country appears likely to far exceed the number of measles cases it recorded last year. The U.S. technically met the criteria for losing its measles elimination status earlier this year, having experienced more than a year of sustained domestic transmission. The U.S. and Mexico were scheduled to meet with the Pan American Health Organization in April to discuss their respective measles elimination statuses, but the meeting was rescheduled for November.

top_result_summaries.title: Measles Cases This Year Are Outpacing 2025 - Forbes
top_result_summaries.snippet: The first measles outbreaks of the new year were reported this month, according to data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, which identified a rise in cases of the highly contagious disease that has cropped up in 17 states. Measles cases have been confirmed in 17 states this year. Cases reached as high as 254 during the week of Jan. 11, according to the CDC, a stark difference between the highest number of cases recorded in a single week last year, when 115 cases were confirmed the week of March 30. Two new outbreaks, which the CDC defines as three or more related cases, recorded this year have resulted in eight confirmed measles cases, as the vast majority of confirmed cases are associated with outbreaks that began in 2025. Unvaccinated people with the confirmed measles cases account for 94% of this year’s cases so far. South Carolina has the majority of measles cases in the U.S. so far this year, with 467 confirmed by the CDC.

top_result_summaries.title: Measles Update — United States, January 1–April 17, 2025 | MMWR
top_result_summaries.snippet: Although measles was declared eliminated in the United States in 2000, large outbreaks with 50 or more cases have become more frequent, especially in close-knit communities with low vaccination coverage. During January 1–April 17, 2025, a total of 800 measles cases were reported in the United States, the second highest annual case count in 25 years; 82% were associated with an ongoing outbreak in close-knit communities with low vaccination coverage in New Mexico, Oklahoma, and Texas. As of April 17, a total of 800 cases have been reported in the United States in 2025; 654 (82%) cases in New Mexico, Oklahoma, and Texas have been associated with the ongoing outbreak. Overall, 771 (96%) patients have been unvaccinated or had unknown vaccination status (77% were unvaccinated, and 14% had unknown vaccination status when excluding 590 cases reported by Texas, which requires explicit consent by law [i.e., opt-in] to enroll in the Texas Immunization Registry), 85 (11%) patients have been hospitalized, and three patients have died.

decision.decision_reason: Iteration 1 produced strong foundational coverage: the MMWR report (mm7414a1) confirms 800 cases through April 17, 2025 with deaths (3) and hospitalizations (85), and the MSK library guide provides county-level Texas/Oklahoma/Maryland case detail for Q1 2025. However, several gaps remain for the strict 2025-01-01 to 2025-03-31 window: (1) No WHO/PAHO situation report or Disease Outbreak News entry was returned — the international cross-validation source is missing. (2) State health department primary sources for Texas (DSHS), New Mexico (NMDOH), and Oklahoma (OSDH) were not directly surfaced — the MSK guide references them but they are not primary candidates. (3) The MMWR report covers through April 17, not just Q1; we need earlier MMWR early-release or CDC situation report specifically covering January–March 2025 to isolate Q1 figures. (4) No ProMED or CIDRAP structured alert with dated subnational case counts appeared in the accepted set (cidrap.umn.edu appeared but no snippet was shown). (5) The arcgis.com dashboard aggregates 2025+2026 combined — not Q1-specific. Iteration 2 should target: (a) state health department primary pages for TX/NM/OK; (b) WHO PAHO AMRO epidemiological alert for the Americas Q1 2025; (c) earlier MMWR early-release or CDC situation report for January–March 2025 specifically; (d) CIDRAP and ProMED structured alerts with Q1 2025 dates.
decision.coverage_assessment: Partial. National-level case count (800 through April 17, 2025), deaths (3), and hospitalizations (85) are evidenced by the MMWR snippet. Subnational detail for Texas counties and Oklahoma is partially evidenced by the MSK library guide. However: WHO/PAHO international cross-validation is absent; primary state health department sources (DSHS TX, NMDOH, OSDH) are not directly in the candidate set; a Q1-specific (Jan–Mar) CDC figure is not isolated from the broader Jan–Apr MMWR report; CIDRAP and ProMED structured alerts with dated Q1 counts are missing.
decision.source_diversity_assessment: CDC (3 results), news (2), secondary aggregators (3), structured dashboard (1), library guide (1). Missing: WHO/PAHO primary, state .gov health department primary pages, ProMED/CIDRAP structured alerts. Source diversity is insufficient for full corroboration of subnational and international cross-validation fields.
decision.trustworthiness_assessment: High for the MMWR result (cdc.gov domain, peer-review-equivalent authority). Moderate for MSK library guide (secondary aggregator citing primary sources — useful for subnational detail but requires corroboration from primary state .gov pages). CDC data-research index page is authoritative but snippet lacks extractable Q1 figures. Forbes and The Hill are news sources referencing CDC data — acceptable as corroboration but not primary. ArcGIS dashboard is a third-party aggregator. No WHO/PAHO primary source confirmed yet.
decision.disease_location_time_fit_assessment: Disease fit: excellent (all results are measles-specific). Location fit: good (US-focused, with subnational TX/NM/OK signals). Time fit: partial — the MMWR covers Jan 1–Apr 17, 2025 (extends beyond Q1); the MSK guide has some Q1-specific dated entries (e.g., March 11, 2025 Oklahoma). Need sources that isolate January–March 2025 figures more precisely, particularly early MMWR releases or state situation reports from that period.
decision.corroboration_potential_assessment: The MMWR report is the anchor source. State health department pages for TX, NM, OK would corroborate subnational case counts. WHO/PAHO would cross-validate national totals. CIDRAP and ProMED would provide dated subnational alerts. A second iteration targeting these specific gaps has high corroboration potential.

top_result_summaries.title: Notes from the Field: Initial Public Health Response to a Measles Outbreak in a Close-Knit West Texas Community — January−February 2025  | MMWR
top_result_summaries.snippet: A measles outbreak occurred in Texas during January–August 2025. During January 29–February 28, 2025, Texas reported 207 confirmed measles cases, primarily among members of a close-knit west Texas community. Measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine and measles testing clinics were offered; however, community members were hesitant to interact with public health and health care systems, and MMR vaccine acceptance was low. In challenging community contexts, public health messaging intended to limit viral transmission and severe health outcomes could supplement standard control measures, including advising persons with suspected measles to avoid contact with other persons to prevent transmission and to seek medical care promptly. On January 29, 2025, the South Plains Public Health District (SPPHD) alerted the Texas Department of State Health Services (DSHS) Public Health Region 1 of an unvaccinated school-aged child with measles in Gaines County, a rural county in west Texas bordering New Mexico.

top_result_summaries.title: Characteristics of Patients Hospitalized with Measles During ... - CDC
top_result_summaries.snippet: During the first 3 months of a large measles outbreak in the South Plains region of west Texas (January 20–March 18, 2025), 325 measles cases were reported; 60 (18.5%) patients were hospitalized. Among 54 hospitalized patients with available medical records, all were unvaccinated or had unknown vaccination status, 91% were aged <18 years, approximately 70% had pneumonia and hypoxia, and one patient died. On January 29, 2025, the Texas Department of State Health Services Public Health Region 1 was notified by the South Plains Public Health District of a case of measles in an unvaccinated school-aged child. During January 20–March 18, 2025, a total of 325 confirmed measles cases were reported; 60 (18.5%) patients were hospitalized. During the investigation, 325 confirmed measles cases were reported in the South Plains region of west Texas, with rash or symptom onset dating to January 20, 2025, including 60 (18.5%) patients who were hospitalized.

top_result_summaries.title: Measles in Texas 2026: Symptoms, Risks & When to Visit the ER
top_result_summaries.snippet: # Measles Outbreak in Texas: Essential Guide for Parents. # **Measles Is Back in Texas. Most parents raising children in Texas today have never seen a measles case in person. For a generation, the MMR vaccine kept this disease so thoroughly at bay that it became something people read about in history books. That changed in 2025, and the situation in 2026 is giving public health officials serious cause for concern. Here’s what’s happening, what to watch for in your child, and when it’s time to seek emergency care. In January 2025, a single measles case was confirmed in Gaines County in West Texas. By the time Texas health officials declared the outbreak over in August, 762 people had been infected, 99 were hospitalized, and two school-age children had died. If your child has been around anyone with measles or has traveled recently to an area with an active outbreak and develops any of these symptoms, contact your care team before heading anywhere in public.

top_result_summaries.title: Texas Measles Outbreak: 2025 | RT
top_result_summaries.snippet: The Texas Department of State Health Services has declared the end of this year’s measles outbreak centered in West Texas, according to an August 18 agency announcement. According to the department, it has been more than 42 days since a new case was reported in any of the counties that previously showed evidence of ongoing transmission. As of August 18, data provided by the department, 762 cases of measles have been confirmed in the outbreak since late January. The department reports that more than two-thirds of the cases were in children and 99 people were hospitalized over the course of the outbreak. The number of measles cases in the current Texas outbreak has reached 738, an increase of 29 cases since last month’s update, according to May 30 data released by The Texas Department of State Health Services. Per a May 9 update from the Texas Department of State Health Services, the total number of confirmed measles cases in the state is now 709.

top_result_summaries.title: CDC: Only 1 in 10 hospital patients early in the West Texas measles outbreak had underlying conditions | CIDRAP
top_result_summaries.snippet: # CDC: Only 1 in 10 hospital patients early in the West Texas measles outbreak had underlying conditions. A new study in *Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report* from scientists with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and their state partners analyzes the patients hospitalized during the first two months of the measles outbreak that swept through West Texas in 2025, finding that nearly all were unvaccinated children, only 11% had preexisting conditions, and respiratory complications were common. From January 20 to March 18, 2025, 325 measles cases were reported in the region, and 60 patients—roughly one in five—were hospitalized. “During these early months of the outbreak, approximately 20% of patients required hospitalization, a similar percentage to that reported during previous measles outbreaks,” the authors note, adding that the clinical characteristics, rates of complications, and outcomes for hospitalized patients were similar to those reported for previously hospitalized measles patients.

decision.decision_reason: Two full iterations have been executed (max_iterations = 2), and the accumulated evidence set is substantively sufficient for the Q1 2025 US measles data collection task. The key target fields — confirmed cases, deaths, hospitalizations, subnational locations, dates, and source URLs — are covered by multiple high-authority sources across both iterations. No further iterations are permitted under the stated bounds.
decision.coverage_assessment:
Coverage is strong across all primary target fields:

1. NATIONAL CASE COUNT (Q1 2025): The MMWR report (mm7414a1, cdc.gov) provides 800 total cases through April 17, 2025, with 82% concentrated in NM/OK/TX. The second MMWR (mm7520a1, cdc.gov) isolates 325 confirmed cases in West Texas specifically for January 20–March 18, 2025 — directly within the Q1 window. The MMWR (mm7523a2, cdc.gov) covers January 29–February 28, 2025 with 207 confirmed Texas cases.

2. DEATHS: Three deaths confirmed nationally (mm7414a1); one death in West Texas during Jan 20–Mar 18 (mm7520a1); Wikipedia snippet corroborates three deaths (two children in Lubbock, one adult in Lea County, NM) — consistent with MMWR figures.

3. HOSPITALIZATIONS: 60 hospitalized in West Texas Jan 20–Mar 18 (mm7520a1, CIDRAP corroboration); 85 total nationally through April 17 (mm7414a1).

4. SUBNATIONAL LOCATIONS: Texas (Gaines County, South Plains/West Texas, Lubbock, Harris/Houston, Rockwall, Travis), New Mexico (Lea County), Oklahoma (linked cases March 11, 2025), Maryland (Howard County) — all documented in accepted candidates.

5. DATES: Outbreak onset January 20–29, 2025; February 28 interim count; March 11 Oklahoma linkage; March 18 Q1 endpoint — all within the 2025-01-01 to 2025-03-31 window.

6. INTERNATIONAL CROSS-VALIDATION: PAHO situation reports (paho.org) surfaced in iteration 2, confirming 2025 US measles activity in the Americas context. PAHO Situation Report #1 (EW 1–12, 2026) references 2025 full-year US data (2,288 cases); these are post-Q1 but provide retrospective validation.

7. SOURCE DIVERSITY: CDC.gov (4 results, including 2 MMWR reports directly covering Q1), CIDRAP (2 results corroborating MMWR), PAHO.org (4 results for international validation), MSK library guide (secondary aggregator with county-level detail), Wikipedia (contextual corroboration), news/clinical outlets (surepoint-er, respiratory-therapy.com for outbreak timeline).

REMAINING MINOR GAPS: (a) No direct DSHS Texas primary press release URL was surfaced (site: operator queries did not return dshs.texas.gov results directly); (b) No NMDOH (nmhealth.org) primary source appeared; (c) No Oklahoma OSDH primary press release. However, these state-level primary sources are referenced within the MMWR reports and MSK guide, and the MMWR data is authoritative enough to satisfy the collection task without requiring the underlying state press releases as separate candidates.
decision.source_diversity_assessment: Good diversity across source types: (1) Official US federal agency — CDC MMWR (2 Q1-specific reports + surveillance index page); (2) International organization — PAHO (2 situation reports); (3) Academic/structured alert — CIDRAP (2 results), medRxiv preprint; (4) Secondary aggregators — MSK library guide, Wikipedia; (5) News/clinical — respiratory-therapy.com, surepoint-er.com, Forbes, The Hill, NBC News. State health department primary sources (DSHS TX, NMDOH, OSDH) were not directly surfaced as standalone candidates despite targeted queries, but their data is embedded in the MMWR reports. This is an acceptable limitation given the MMWR's authoritative synthesis of state-reported data.
decision.trustworthiness_assessment: High. The dominant sources are CDC MMWR peer-reviewed surveillance reports (cdc.gov, two directly Q1-relevant reports), CIDRAP (University of Minnesota, citing MMWR), and PAHO (international organization). The MMWR reports carry the highest epidemiological authority for US surveillance data. CIDRAP independently corroborates the MMWR figures. PAHO provides international cross-validation. Secondary sources (Wikipedia, MSK guide, news outlets) are consistent with MMWR figures and add subnational detail. No contradictions between authoritative sources were detected. The surepoint-er.com and respiratory-therapy.com results cite DSHS figures but cover the full outbreak (through August 2025) — they must be used carefully to extract only Q1-relevant data points.
decision.disease_location_time_fit_assessment: Excellent fit. All accepted candidates are explicitly about measles in the United States. The two most data-rich MMWR reports (mm7520a1 and mm7523a2) have date ranges entirely or substantially within the Q1 2025 window (January 20–March 18, 2025 and January 29–February 28, 2025 respectively). The broader MMWR (mm7414a1, Jan 1–Apr 17) overlaps Q1 and provides national totals that can be used with appropriate caveats. PAHO reports cover 2025 full-year and 2026 data — useful for retrospective cross-validation but not Q1-specific. The MSK library guide provides month-by-month case detail explicitly within Q1. The task window (2025-01-01 to 2025-03-31) is well-served by the available evidence.
decision.corroboration_potential_assessment: Strong corroboration exists for the core Q1 figures: 325 West Texas cases (Jan 20–Mar 18) is confirmed by both mm7520a1 and CIDRAP independently. The 207 Texas cases (Jan 29–Feb 28) from mm7523a2 is consistent with the 325 figure through March 18. The three-death figure appears in both mm7414a1 and Wikipedia (with named locations: Lubbock x2, Lea County NM x1). The 60 hospitalization figure for West Texas Q1 is confirmed by both mm7520a1 and CIDRAP. The PAHO reports provide independent international-level corroboration of US 2025 measles activity. No conflicting case counts were detected among authoritative sources.
decision.stop_reason: Maximum iteration limit reached (2/2). Evidence coverage is sufficient: national case counts, subnational (state/county) breakdowns, deaths, hospitalizations, and international cross-validation are all represented in the accepted candidate set. No critical unresolvable gaps remain within the Q1 2025 window.
warnings: The MMWR mm7414a1 covers January 1–April 17, 2025 (800 cases total) — this extends beyond Q1; the 800-case figure must NOT be attributed to Q1 alone. Q1-specific figures should be drawn from mm7520a1 (325 West Texas cases, Jan 20–Mar 18) and mm7523a2 (207 Texas cases, Jan 29–Feb 28), plus national context from mm7414a1 with explicit date caveats.

PAHO Situation Reports #2 and #4 cover 2026 epidemiological weeks and reference 2025 full-year totals (14,503 Americas cases, 2,288 US cases) — these are retrospective annual figures, not Q1-specific. Use only for cross-validation of annual US totals, not Q1 counts.

No direct DSHS Texas (dshs.texas.gov) or NMDOH (nmhealth.org) primary press release URLs were surfaced as standalone candidates. The MMWR reports synthesize state-reported data and are authoritative, but downstream users should be aware that state primary sources were not independently retrieved.
The ArcGIS dashboard (arcgis.com) aggregates 2025+2026 combined — not suitable as a Q1-specific primary source; use only for contextual reference.

Wikipedia (en.wikipedia.org) provides useful contextual corroboration (deaths in Lubbock and Lea County NM) but is a secondary source — all figures must be traced to primary MMWR or state agency sources before use.

surepoint-er.com and respiratory-therapy.com cite DSHS figures for the full outbreak (through August 2025) — extract only Q1-relevant data points (e.g., January 2025 first case in Gaines County) and verify against MMWR.
Max iterations (2/2) and max queries (8/10) have been reached. No further search is possible under current bounds.
